blocks.x: Pediculosis is infestation of the body, head hair, or pubic hair by the obligate insect parasite — lice. All three types are ectoparasites (live on the host's surface), move by crawling, have humans as their only host, and share similar life cycles.

items: Pediculus humanus humanus — Body Louse ("clothing louse", "grey back", "mechanized dandruff"). Causes pediculosis corporis.
Pediculus humanus capitis — Head Louse. Causes pediculosis capitis.
Pthirus pubis — Pubic Louse ("crab louse"). Causes pediculosis pubis, or pediculosis ciliaris if it infests eyelashes.

sections.title: Body louse morphology, and how the pubic louse differs

blocks.x: The body louse: grey, small (2–4mm), wingless (an ectoparasitic adaptation), soft with a translucent leathery integument, flattened dorsoventrally, inconspicuous laterally-placed simple eyes, short 5-segmented antennae, and 3 pairs of stout, well-developed legs. The abdomen has 9 segments with sclerotised lateral margins; females have a bifurcated "V"/"W" gonopod, males a penis. Spiracles sit on the thorax and abdomen.

Mouthparts are modified for piercing and sucking: a short tubular flexible haustellum, a labrum with tiny teeth, and a stylet sac containing the stabbing apparatus — 1 dorsal hypopharynx, 1 dorsal mandible stylet, 2 ventral maxillae stylets, and a gutter-shaped labium.

The pubic louse is smaller than the other two, with less differentiation between thorax and abdomen — broad and squat. The 1st leg pair is small and slender, but the 2nd and 3rd pairs bear massive claws, giving it a sluggish, crab-like movement — hence "crab louse."

Three life stages: egg/nit, nymph (3 moults), adult. Both nymphs and adults take blood meals. Nits are oval and white with an operculum (small lid), firmly cemented in place; 200–300 eggs are laid per lifetime; the egg stage lasts 6–10 days.

Body lice feed day and night, live in clothes (adults/nymphs live permanently on man), attracted by odour, sweat chemistry, body temperature, humidity, and darkness. 6–9 eggs glued to clothing daily; gregarious, found in seams. Incomplete metamorphosis: 3 nymphal instars over 7–14 days each, maturity reached in 16–27 days, adults live ~1 month. In heavy infestations, up to 10,000 lice and nits may be found on one person.
Head lice: biology similar to body lice. Female lays ~6–8 eggs/day (~300 lifetime), hatching in 7–10 days; 3 nymphal instars.

Pubic lice: eggs hatch in 8 days, ~200 laid per lifetime, cemented to coarse genital/perianal hairs. Prefer a humid atmosphere; avoid the scalp (hair too dense). Transmitted through sexual contact — "papillons d'amour."

sections.title: Epidemiology and transmission by louse type

blocks.x: Body louse — associated with poverty, poor hygiene, crowding. Transmitted by direct or indirect contact (clothing); adults are 2–4mm, live and lay eggs in clothing seams, and can survive up to 3 days without a host.
Head louse — children most commonly affected, females more than males. Direct or indirect contact (fomites); adults 2–3mm; females live 1 month, laying 7–10 nits/day, cementing nits at the hair base.

Pubic louse — sexually active young adults. Transmitted through sexual activity (fomite transmission less likely). Contact with eyes can cause pediculosis ciliaris. Adult crab louse is 0.8–1.2mm; females live 3–4 weeks, laying ~3 nits/day.

sections.title: The itch, and what follows it

blocks.x: Head louse: not a vector of any disease. General complaint is the itch; secondary infections may set in.

Pubic louse: does not transmit disease. Itch occurs only in infested areas; severe allergic reaction possible from saliva. May spread from the pubic area to the perineum, thighs, umbilicus, chest, moustache, beard, and eyelashes.

Body louse: intense pruritis from an allergic reaction to lice saliva (sensitization can take 4–6 weeks), producing a morbilliform rash. Excoriations, possible lymphadenopathy, and secondary bacterial infections like impetigo may follow. Critically, body lice can transmit bacterial infections — unlike head or pubic lice.

Caused by Borrelia recurrentis. Acute infection with a 2–14 day (~6 day) incubation period, followed by recurring febrile episodes (headaches, chills, fever, muscle aches). Also known as Epidemic Relapsing Fever, associated with poverty, crowding, and warfare — with low mortality.

Transmitted person-to-person by human body lice from an infected reservoir — but only when the louse is injured (e.g. during scratching), so a single louse can only infect a single person. Notably, lice leave a febrile host to seek a host with normal body temperature — aiding spread.

Louse-Borne Typhus Fever is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii. When a bacteremic patient is bitten, the organism is ingested and multiplies in the louse's gut epithelium, then is excreted in faeces during the next bite — the person autoinoculates themselves by scratching the bite site. Untreated cases may die from peripheral vascular collapse or bacterial pneumonia, with severe meningo-encephalitis (delirium, coma) in complications.
Trench Fever is caused by Rickettsia quintana — not fatal, but can be incapacitating.
Body louse: delousing, hot water and hot air, ironing, fumigation, good hygiene — or shaving plus 5% DDT dust spray.
Head louse: removal is a co-operative task using insecticidal formulations (shampoos, DDT dust), hot combs, or shaving in severe cases.

Bed bugs belong to Order Hemiptera (true bugs — the largest order of Exopterygote insects), Family Cimicidae. Two species: Cimex lectularius (temperate zone, the "human bed bug," cosmopolitan) and Cimex hemipterus (tropical zone, the "tropical bed bug").

Nicknamed "red coats," "mahogany flats," "wall louse." Temporary ectoparasites — obligate haematophagous insects — parasites of man almost exclusively, occasionally feeding on birds, bats, and rodents.
Adults: oval, wingless with vestigial wings (hemielytra), pale yellow/brown unfed → mahogany when fed, flattened dorsoventrally, short and broad ("squat") body.

Head: short and broad, prominent laterally-placed compound eyes, 4-segmented antennae, 3-segmented proboscis appressed to the ventral surface. Thorax: prothorax larger than meso/metathorax, with lateral flanges; rudimentary wings lie over the meso/metathorax; 3 pairs of walking legs with stink pads. Abdomen: lemon-shaped, 8 visible segments; males have a well-developed curved penis; females have a small genital pouch (4th segment) housing the organ of Berlese/Ribaga (mesospermalege) which collects and stores sperm.

sections.title: Bed bug life cycle: hemimetabolous and resilient

blocks.x: Both sexes feed on blood especially at night; they hide in cracks and crevices by day, are gregarious, and return to harbourages by following pheromone chemical trails.

Eggs: whitish/yellow, curved anteriorly, vase-shaped, covered with a gelatinous secretion that fixes them in cracks, with a small operculum. 6–10 eggs laid per week, hatching after 8–11 days. Females live many weeks/months, laying 150–500 eggs in a lifetime. Life cycle is hemimetabolous.
5 nymphal instars, pale yellow, closely resembling adults; each instar needs at least one blood meal; they defecate as they feed, leaving rust-like blood stains on sheets. Nymphal period: 5–8 weeks.

Adults can live 1–4 years, survive over 500 days of starvation, and can semi-hibernate with high desiccation tolerance. Mating is unique — traumatic insemination — with sperm stored in the spermatheca (copulatory pouch).
Presence is recognized by: cast-off nymph skins, hatched/unhatched eggs, small dark marks on clothing/bedding, skin rash/small blisters, and a sickly sweet smell — like rotting raspberries.

Adults have limited dispersal power, easily carried in clothing, bedding, furniture, luggage. They don't tarry on clothes, so they defecate on bedding. They bite exposed surfaces (not through clothing) and travel several feet for a meal — associated with low hygiene and overcrowding.

Bed bugs are not natural vectors of any human disease, though they may transmit hepatitis B mechanically via faeces. The bite condition is called Cimicosis — painful, causing irritation and swelling. Nocturnal blood-sucking disrupts sleep, and repeated close-together bites can cause distress, anaemia, nervousness, insomnia, nausea, vomiting, chills, and iron deficiency in children.
Three approaches: structure proofing (sealing cracks, crevices, gaps); chemical control (fumigation, residual insecticides); and other measures like impregnated bed nets.

Practical elimination steps: carefully remove items from the room; spray small items and bag them; dismantle and spray bed frames; remove and spray drawers/wardrobes; spray/soak mattresses with insecticide and cover with large mattress encasements over seams and folds; seal holes, cracks, and crevices (change wallpaper if needed); send bed linen to laundry; vacuum carpets, discarding and burning heavily infested ones.

Lice and bed bugs are both ectoparasites tied closely to poverty, crowding, and poor hygiene — but they differ sharply in disease risk. Body lice are genuine disease vectors (relapsing fever, typhus); head and pubic lice cause nuisance disease only; bed bugs cause distressing bites but are not confirmed vectors of any human disease at all. Recognizing which is which shapes both the clinical response and the public health priority.

lines: Body louse (P. h. humanus) - pediculosis corporis - DOES transmit disease
Head louse (P. h. capitis) - pediculosis capitis - no disease, just itch
Pubic louse (Pthirus pubis) - pediculosis pubis/ciliaris - sexual transmission
Relapsing Fever: Borrelia recurrentis, via crushed louse
Typhus: Rickettsia prowazekii, via scratched-in faeces
Trench Fever: Rickettsia quintana, not fatal
Hemimetabolous, 5 nymphal instars, each needs 1 blood meal
Adults live 1-4 years, survive 500+ days starvation
NOT a confirmed disease vector - bites cause Cimicosis
Bed bugs: sweet "rotting raspberry" smell, rust-coloured faecal spots on sheets
